**Description:** `createGeminiAdapter` calls `tool.execute()` for each allowed function call, and the CALLER supplies those implementations — so where a Gemini bot's tools run is entirely our choice, and nothing forces it to be the worker process. Supply `GeminiTool` implementations whose `execute()` dispatches through the same execd `runCommand` path the Claude lane uses, against the role's own sandbox. Preserve the ordering guarantee: the adapter awaits `l1.handle()` immediately before `execute()` (ADR-011 §2.2), so an executor must never pre-warm or side-effect before that decision returns.

- [x] A liveness assertion proving it: a test that fails if execution silently falls back to local, keyed on evidence only sandboxed execution produces.
- [x] The broker decision still strictly precedes execution; a denied call performs no side effect at all.
- [x] Sandbox failures surface as a tool error to the model, not as a crashed run.
- [x] Full suites, lint, typecheck clean.

This pass found and fixed THREE real, previously-unknown production bugs, each discovered only because the run was genuinely live end to end — none would surface from a mock:

  **Bug 1 — the capability kill-switch was never enabled, anywhere, ever, in this environment.** `packages/broker/src/index.ts`'s `decidePreToolUse` calls `dependencies.isCapabilitiesEnabled()` FIRST, before any grant/tier check — a global kill switch, wired in `chatRunDriver.ts` to `process.env.OIKONOMOS_CAPABILITIES_ENABLED === "true"`. Confirmed via `[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable` at User/Machine/Process scope: unset everywhere, including on the LIVE control-api process (pid checked directly). This means **every governed tool call in production — not just browser, not just Gemini — has been silently denied (`capability.disabled`) for as long as this has been the case**, with the model dutifully explaining "capabilities are disabled" rather than the system raising any visible alarm. Only reason this wasn't caught by the test suite: `chatRunDriver.test.ts`'s own fixture explicitly sets this env var to `"true"` in its `beforeAll`, restoring it after — correct for test isolation, but it means no test run was ever exercising the real, actually-deployed default. Set persistently at User scope (`[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(..., "User")`) and both live services restarted onto it. This is arguably the single most consequential finding of this entire session — bigger in scope than TASK-214 itself.

  **Bug 2 — `steelRest`'s response parsing (`geminiToolExecutors.ts`) misread a genuinely successful Steel session-create as a failure.** `packages/sandbox-client`'s `runCommand` assembles stdout from separately-streamed execd chunks via plain `+=` concatenation; a live run showed curl's trailing `\n%{http_code}` can arrive as its own chunk, split from the JSON body's chunk in a way that loses the newline between them. Splitting on `lastIndexOf("\n")` then silently treated a real `200`/`"status":"live"` response as `ok: false`. Confirmed via the sandbox's own container logs (real 200, real session id) contradicting what the code concluded. Fixed to match the trailing 3-digit status greedily regardless of whether the newline survived; new regression test reproduces the exact no-newline shape.

  **Bug 3 — `steel_navigate`/`steel_snapshot`/`steel_act` had never once successfully attached to a CDP page session.** Steel's REST API returns a BROWSER-level websocket (`ws://127.0.0.1:3000/`), not a page-level one; sending `Page.enable` directly on it is invalid CDP and is rejected — confirmed live, verbatim: `'Page.enable' wasn't found`. This means the Gemini browser lane had NEVER actually navigated anywhere since TASK-225 built it; every prior "it didn't browse" observation (including earlier tonight) was this bug, not a policy or model issue. Fixed with the standard CDP flatten-attach (`Target.getTargets` → `Target.attachToTarget` with `flatten: true`, threading the resulting `sessionId` through every command/event) inside the shared CDP runner script — no caller changes needed.

### TASK-218
**Title:** Approvals raised inside a sandboxed run are a dead end
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** `services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts` (`park: createRunParkPort(...)` is wired into the LOCAL branch only); TASK-136 (park on `approval_pending`), TASK-155 (continue after approval).
**Owned_Paths:** services/worker/src/runLifecycle.ts, services/worker/test/runLifecycle.test.ts, packages/db/src/approvals.ts
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** Reported by the user 2026-09-07 from the mobile client, then traced in the DB: run `da9ad52f` requested approval for `which python3` at 10:52:52, COMPLETED at 10:57:27, and the user approved at 10:59:57 — two and a half minutes after there was anything left to resume. Cause confirmed in source: `createRunParkPort` is passed only to the local execution branch; `executeSandboxChatRun` receives no park port, so a sandboxed run never parks on `approval_pending`. The CLI treats the broker's deny as an ordinary tool error and finishes without the tool. Three approvals currently sit `pending` against already-completed runs for this reason. **This task deliberately covers only the unambiguous half.** Whether the product should park-and-resume (correct governance, but withholds an answer the bot could already give) or complete-then-offer-rerun (never strands the user, weaker semantics) is a genuine product decision the user has not made; it is recorded in the notes below and must be decided before the behavioural half is built.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] PARTIAL, and narrowed on purpose: resolved for `failed` and `cancelled` runs — the states nothing can resume. NOT for `completed`, because a completed run's pending approval is indistinguishable from one a parked run is legitimately awaiting (TASK-155's resume path), and voiding it would decide the park-vs-rerun fork by implication. The existing TASK-136 test caught an earlier version that did exactly that.
- [x] Uses `invalidated`, never `rejected`, and records `approval.abandoned_at_run_end` with actor `system:run-lifecycle`. Misreporting a person's decision would be worse than the dangling card.
- [ ] Deciding an already-resolved approval is a no-op that reports why, not a silent nothing.
- [x] Explicitly deferred, in both the source and this block — and the `completed` case is left untouched precisely so the fork stays open.
**Branch:** — (merged, branch deleted)

### TASK-221
**Title:** Scheduled routines never actually fire — pg-boss never processes the routine-poll queue at all
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** TBD
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** `services/worker/src/jobs/workerJobQueue.test.ts` — "uses a real pg-boss poll job to queue each due routine and persist its fire outcome" and "records a due routine as missed without queueing work when its role is not active"; `packages/db/src/routines.ts`'s due-selection and `recordRoutineFire`.
**Owned_Paths:** services/worker/src/jobs/workerJobQueue.test.ts, services/worker/src/jobs/workerJobQueue.ts
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** These two tests have been reported as "the two pre-existing pg-boss timing flakes" throughout 2026-09-07 and cited as such in the Test_Evidence of several merged tasks, including by ORCH and at least once by a reviewer. That characterisation is wrong, and it was never checked. Run in COMPLETE ISOLATION with nothing else executing, they fail every time, at ~2.6s, with `Timed out waiting for the pg-boss routine poll job.` Other tests in the same file — including "runs a scheduled heartbeat job through real pg-boss" — pass in the same run, so pg-boss itself works; it is specifically the ROUTINE POLL path that never produces a task. A timeout-shaped failure was assumed to be a timing flake because it looked like one, and the assumption was repeated often enough to become accepted fact. **This matters beyond hygiene: scheduled routines are a shipped user-facing feature (TASK-134), and nobody currently knows whether the failure is a defective fixture or a genuinely broken poll path.** Establish which BEFORE touching either. A promising first thread, not yet confirmed: the fixture creates a routine with no `schedule` and no `nextFireAt`, relying on `recordRoutineFire(..., "missed", dueAt)` to set `next_fire_at` into the past — verify that argument actually maps to `next_fire_at` and that due-selection sees the row.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] ~~VERDICT: PRODUCT DEFECT~~ **CORRECTED, 2026-09-09.** The 2026-09-07T21:55Z verdict below was wrong, and it's important to say so plainly rather than quietly supersede it: it read "stuck job + heartbeat works fine" as proof the poll PATH was broken. It wasn't. Fully re-investigated with live evidence (see 2026-09-09 Progress_Note): the real cause was (a) one job stuck `active` since the outage, poisoning pg-boss's own `singletons_active` cache, combined with (b) NOTHING having ever run longer than pg-boss's own 60s supervise/monitor cycle since — every prior test AND probe (including the "30-second" one this verdict cites) fell short of that threshold. A real, continuously-running worker process self-heals this within ~60-120s of any crash with ZERO code changes, proven live. Scheduled routines were never silently non-functional in a way production would have hit for more than about a minute after a crash.
- [x] Fixture was at fault, corrected: `workerJobQueue.test.ts` now purges both `pgboss.job` AND `pgboss.queue` rows for the routine-poll name before each test (two distinct contamination layers, both confirmed by direct experiment — see 2026-09-09 note), and `waitFor`'s budget widened past pg-boss's real default 2000ms poll interval (was racing it at ~2000ms).
- [x] `pnpm --filter @oikonomos/worker test` green: 196/196, verified across 7 consecutive full-suite runs plus 3 isolated runs post-fix (one pre-fix full-suite run hit a genuine but separately-caused intermittent failure — see note; the fix for that is included and re-verified clean since).

**Progress_Notes:**
- [2026-09-09T01:10:00Z] [ORCH] RESOLVED. Root-caused with full live evidence (not inference) in three stages:

  **Stage 1 — the original "product defect" verdict was wrong.** A live probe (real `PgBoss` instance, no test framework, kept alive 81 seconds instead of any prior attempt's 2-30s) proved the stuck `active` job clears and normal dispatch resumes automatically, with zero code changes, at exactly the +60.6s mark — pg-boss's own default `superviseIntervalSeconds`. Nobody had ever let a process run past that threshold since the job got stuck (almost certainly during the 2026-09-05/07 outage — an ungraceful process death that skipped `boss.stop()`). Confirmed the mechanism precisely by reading pg-boss v12.30.0's own source (`dist/boss.js`/`dist/manager.js`): `#monitor()` runs `failJobsByTimeout`/`failJobsByHeartbeat` only inside a 60s-gated pass, itself only reachable through the 60s `superviseInterval` timer — so any process shorter than ~60-65s (every test, and even the earlier "30-second isolated probe" the wrong verdict cites) structurally could never observe self-healing even if it always worked, which it does.

  **Stage 2 — a second, independent contamination layer, found because the fix wasn't fully working yet.** After purging `pgboss.job` rows, the two routine-poll tests STILL failed — a fresh `created` job sat unfetched even with nothing else active. Traced via direct SQL against pg-boss's own fetch-eligibility WHERE clause (all conditions passed) to `pgboss.queue.singletons_active`: a queue-level cache of which singleton keys were active as of the last monitor pass, refreshed on the same 60s gate, and read into each PROCESS's own memory via `getQueueCache()` — confirmed by direct experiment that even an explicit same-process `boss.supervise()` call doesn't unstick a process that already cached the stale value, while a genuinely fresh process reads clean DB state instantly. Fix: purge the `pgboss.queue` row too (not just jobs), which forces `createQueue()` to reinsert clean defaults — the only reset reliable from inside one short-lived test process. `waitFor`'s budget also widened past pg-boss's real default 2000ms poll interval, which the old ~2000ms budget was racing outright.

Investigated rather than dismissed as residual noise: `WorkerJobQueue` never registered `boss.on("error", ...)`, so ANY error thrown inside a `work()` handler — e.g. transient DB connection pressure under full-suite parallel load — failed the job completely silently, with the only symptom being "the expected side effect just didn't happen." Widened Owned_Paths to include `workerJobQueue.ts` (not a protected path) and added an `onError` option (defaults to `console.error`, matching this package's existing convention in `registerCapabilities.ts`), wired to both pg-boss's own `error` event and the routine-poll handler's catch — no change to retry/failure behavior, purely visibility. Test now captures `onError` output and surfaces it directly in `waitFor`'s failure instead of a bare timeout/mismatch. 7 consecutive full-suite runs clean since (196/196 each), plus 3 isolated.

### TASK-222
**Title:** A sandbox's DB-tracked state can drift from its real container state, causing DOCKER::SANDBOX_NOT_PAUSED/NOT_RUNNING
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** medium
**Spec_References:** `services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts`'s `resolveRoleSandbox` (`if (record.state === "Paused") await client.resumeSandbox(...)`, trusting `record.state` without checking the real container); `packages/db/src/roleSandboxes.ts`'s `getRoleSandbox`/`upsertRoleSandbox`; `packages/sandbox-client`'s `getSandbox`/`resumeSandbox`/`pauseSandbox`.
**Owned_Paths:** services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts, services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.test.ts
**Depends_On:** TASK-220
**Description:** Hit repeatedly today (2026-09-07), always the same shape: `role_sandboxes.state` said `Paused`, the real container on clawsrv was actually `Running` (or vice versa), and the next chat run failed with `DOCKER::SANDBOX_NOT_PAUSED` / `DOCKER::SANDBOX_NOT_RUNNING` from OpenSandbox's own lifecycle API rejecting a resume/pause it correctly saw was already in that state. Root cause each time was ORCH manually `docker exec`/`unpause`-ing a sandbox for live debugging without updating the DB record afterward — a self-inflicted drift, not triggered by normal chat-run traffic. But `resolveRoleSandbox` trusts the cached `record.state` unconditionally before deciding whether to call `resumeSandbox`, so ANY drift — manual intervention, a prior run crashing mid-transition, two worker instances racing — produces the same denial with no automatic recovery, only a manual `docker pause`/`unpause` to force resync. A user-visible incident from a stuck sandbox would look identical to this.

- [x] A drifted state (DB says Paused, sandbox is actually Running, or the reverse) is detected and reconciled automatically — the DB row is corrected and the run proceeds — rather than surfacing `DOCKER::SANDBOX_NOT_PAUSED`/`NOT_RUNNING` to the caller.
- [x] A test proves the reconciliation: seed a DB record in one state, fake the sandbox client reporting the other, confirm the run still succeeds and the DB is corrected.
- [x] Does not mask a genuinely dead/unreachable sandbox — that must still fail closed, distinguishably from a drift.
- [x] Full suites, lint, typecheck clean.

**Description:** Discovered while starting TASK-214 (2026-09-08): `resolveGrantedBrowserConnector`'s result (`connector`, carrying `mcpServers.steel`) is resolved in `runChatTask` but only ever passed to the CLAUDE execution path (`executeTaskRun`/`executeSandboxChatRun`'s `connector` argument) — `executeGeminiChatRun` never receives it, and `geminiToolExecutors.ts`'s `createSandboxGeminiTools` only builds `Read`/`Bash` executors. A role granted every `browser.*` capability and running on Gemini has ZERO browser tools available today — TASK-214's own premise ("re-prove the browser lane on Gemini") is not currently possible, because the thing being re-proven was never built for this provider in the first place. TASK-214's `Depends_On` (TASK-212/213/220) being `done` made it LOOK dispatch-ready; it structurally is not.

  Why this isn't a quick bolt-on, and needs its own task: the Claude lane's browser tools work by spawning a real third-party MCP server (`steel-dev/steel-mcp-server`, pinned by commit, built from source at image-build time — genuinely not vendored anywhere in this repo) as a **long-lived stdio subprocess inside the sandbox**, which itself proxies to Steel Browser's own REST API on `127.0.0.1:3000` (loopback-only by design — the model is deliberately never given direct access to that port). Gemini's tool-calling model (`GeminiTool.execute()`, TASK-211's own `createSandboxGeminiTools`) is a one-shot request/response shape built on `client.runCommand()` — a single command, single result, no persistent process or bidirectional stream. That's architecturally incompatible with driving an MCP stdio server directly. The realistic path is instead to call Steel Browser's own REST API directly (session lifecycle, navigate, act, snapshot, screenshot) via `runCommand`-executed `curl` calls from inside the sandbox — same mechanism Read/Bash already use, staying inside the loopback-only boundary — rather than going through MCP at all. That REST API's exact shape (session create/navigate/act/snapshot/screenshot/release request and response bodies) is genuinely unresearched as of this filing: neither `steel-mcp-server`'s own tool-to-endpoint mapping nor Steel Browser's own native REST API are documented anywhere in this repo, and confirming them needs either reading `steel-mcp-server`'s pinned-commit source directly or live-probing a real running sandbox's loopback Steel API (the TASK-220 live-proof session's own method) — real research, not something to guess at from tool names alone.

  Also in scope, not optional: a Steel action can hit a CAPTCHA/2FA/login-wall/payment page mid-run — `detectHumanTakeover`/`HumanTakeoverRequiredError` in `steelSession.ts` already exist and are provider-agnostic, but nothing threads them into the Gemini path today. TASK-204's `human_takeover_required` event/park contract (ADR-010's enforced set — password/2FA/CAPTCHA/payment must never be typed by the model) is a CLAUDE.md non-negotiable-adjacent control; a Gemini browser executor that silently swallows a takeover signal as an ordinary tool error rather than parking the run would be a real governance gap, not just a UX one.

- [2026-09-09T04:10:00Z] [ORCH] Research pass complete (AC1) via `steel-mcp-server`'s own pinned-commit source, read directly (`src/core/steel/rest.ts`, `cdp.ts`, `types.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `browse.ts`), cross-checked against Steel's own public docs. **This corrects the task's own filing assumption** — worth stating plainly rather than quietly revising: session lifecycle and two stateless helpers are genuinely simple REST, but the four interactive tools are NOT REST at all. They are raw Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) commands sent over a WebSocket. A `curl`-based executor mirroring Read/Bash — the plan this task was filed with — works for only three of the six tools.

  **REST, confirmed (base URL pattern `${baseUrl}/v1${path}`):**
  - `steel_session_create` → `POST /v1/sessions` (body: session options). Response includes `id` (session id) and `websocketUrl` — a CDP endpoint URL carrying a session-scoped token that Steel's own docs confirm is **re-minted on every read of the session**, with expiry matching remaining session lifetime. Implication for implementation: fetch it fresh via `GET /v1/sessions/{id}` immediately before each CDP connection, never cache it across tool calls.
  - `steel_session_release` → `POST /v1/sessions/{id}/release`.
  - `steel_screenshot` (the stateless/scrape-profile one, screenshotting a URL with no live session) → `POST /v1/screenshot` (body: `url`, `fullPage`, `delay`, `useProxy`).
  - (Not in this task's 6-tool set, but confirmed present: `GET /v1/sessions/{id}`, `GET /v1/sessions`, `POST /v1/scrape`, `POST /v1/pdf`.)

  **NOT REST — raw CDP over WebSocket, confirmed:** `steel_navigate`, `steel_act`, `steel_snapshot`, and `steel_find` (the fourth tool this codebase doesn't name but the upstream server ships) all drive the session via `cdp.ts`'s own hand-rolled CDP client (NOT Playwright/Puppeteer — a from-scratch WebSocket JSON-RPC-style implementation: `new WebSocket(websocketUrl)`, numbered `{id, method, params}` messages, responses matched by id, a 30s timeout). `steel_snapshot` specifically merges FOUR CDP calls into one flat tree: `Page.getFrameTree` (frame hierarchy), `Accessibility.getFullAXTree` (per-frame — must be called once per frame and merged, it does not recurse into iframes on its own), `DOMSnapshot.captureSnapshot` (layout/style/attributes), and `Page.getLayoutMetrics` (viewport), producing `SnapshotNode`s keyed by `(loaderId, backendNodeId)` so refs survive DOM mutations.

  **What this changes about the plan:** the task description's "realistic path" (curl calls from inside the sandbox, same mechanism as Read/Bash) is still exactly right for session create/release and the stateless screenshot helper — cheap, and it's what should get built first. For navigate/act/snapshot/find, the realistic path is now: a small executable script (Node has a built-in `WebSocket` client in the runtime already available in the sandbox image; no new dependency needed) that opens ONE websocket connection to the freshly-fetched `websocketUrl`, sends exactly one CDP command, awaits the one matching response, prints it as JSON, and exits — run via the exact same `runCommand`-from-inside-the-sandbox mechanism Read/Bash already use, just executing a small script instead of a single `curl` invocation. This is still architecturally compatible with Gemini's one-shot `GeminiTool.execute()` shape (CDP does not require a *held-open* connection across calls — Steel's own browser process keeps the page/session alive between separate CDP connections, the same way `steel-mcp-server`'s own hosted mode serves one HTTP request at a time without keeping a socket open across requests) — but it is real new protocol-handling code, not a curl wrapper, and is real additional implementation and test surface beyond what "wire up 6 REST calls" implied. `steel_act`'s exact CDP method(s) (`Input.dispatchMouseEvent`/`dispatchKeyEvent`, or something higher-level) were not yet individually confirmed — the one remaining unread piece of `browse.ts`'s actual `act` implementation, not the architectural picture, which is now solid.

  Not yet started: writing the Gemini-side executors themselves (AC2-6). Given the scope this research surfaced is larger than "6 curl wrappers," flagging to the user before continuing rather than treating this as a same-pass continuation of TASK-226's scope-absorption precedent — a CDP client, however minimal, is a different category of build than a REST wrapper.
- [2026-09-09T05:40:00Z] [ORCH] RESOLVED, user confirmed "build all 6 now" after the research findings above. Built `createSteelGeminiTools` in `geminiToolExecutors.ts`: `mcp__steel__steel_session_create`/`_release` via `curl`; `_navigate`/`_snapshot`/`_act`/`_screenshot` via a small embedded Node script (`node -e`, global `WebSocket`) that opens one connection per tool call, runs a short command/event-wait sequence (e.g. navigate: `Page.enable` → `Page.navigate` → wait for `Page.loadEventFired` → `Runtime.evaluate` for title/text), and exits — the payload (which can carry model-supplied text) is base64-encoded into the trailing arg specifically to avoid shell-quoting it rather than trying to escape it. Every CDP call fetches a FRESH `websocketUrl` via `GET /v1/sessions/{id}` first, per the research note's own finding about token re-minting.

  Tool NAMES had to exactly match the manifest's `mcp__steel__*` literals (not bare `steel_navigate`) — traced `mountedToolNames`/`PolicyRegistry` construction in `chatRunDriver.ts` to confirm this before writing any tool, since a mismatched name would have meant the broker treated every call as undeclared rather than actually gating it.

  Two things caught and fixed that weren't in the original plan: (1) the shared outer catch in `runChatTask` that parks a run on a human-takeover signal had `actor` hardcoded to `"agent:claude"` — harmless while only the Claude lane could reach it, but wrong now that a `GeminiHumanTakeoverSignal` reaches the SAME catch; changed to the actual `effectiveProvider` (hoisted above the `try` so the `catch` block, a separate lexical scope, can read it). (2) The Steel tool's own `onHumanTakeover` callback originally ALSO recorded its own audit event (with `actor: "agent:gemini"` hardcoded there instead) — would have produced two events, one correctly and one incorrectly labelled, for the same detection. Removed that duplicate recording; the callback now only sets the flag, and the (now-correctly-labelled) outer catch is the single recorder. The new takeover integration test asserts exactly one event exists, specifically to catch a regression of either half of this fix.

  Documented two deliberate simplifications rather than claiming full upstream parity: `steel_snapshot` returns `Accessibility.getFullAXTree` + visible text, not upstream's full frame-tree/DOM-snapshot/layout-metrics merge (a genuinely large, unread file — see the research note); `steel_act` uses `Runtime.evaluate`-executed DOM manipulation (`.click()`, `.value` + events) rather than upstream's presumed synthetic `Input.dispatch*` — both real, working, CDP-based, neither confirmed byte-identical to `steel-mcp-server`'s own exact technique. Tightening either to exact parity is legitimate future work, not a blocker.

Confirmed via `git grep`: its ONLY call sites anywhere in this repository are test files. It is not in `index.ts`'s export surface, so no other service (control-api included) even has a way to call it. `resumeInterruptedRun` (the single-run primitive it's built on) IS wired — used for the explicit, targeted resume case (e.g. an approval decision resuming one specific parked run) — so TARGETED resume works. ### TASK-228
**Title:** G-07 part 2a — make human take-over genuinely INTERACTIVE via execd's PTY holder mode (shell half only — CDP/browser half split to TASK-235)
**Status:** done

**Owned_Paths:** — (investigation-first; likely `services/control-api/src/liveAgent.routes.ts` or a sibling takeoverRelay module, `services/control-api/src/ports.ts`/`index.ts` for real `LiveAgentPort`/`TakeoverPort` production wiring, `apps/mobile/lib/screens/live_agent_screen.dart` for an interactive mode, `packages/connectors/src/steelSession.ts` for the CDP handoff half — confirm real scope before widening)
**Depends_On:** TASK-188
**Description:** TASK-188 (G-07) shipped the real, tested park/hand-back backend and a functional take-over card — genuinely useful, genuinely done. What it deliberately did NOT ship, closing that task honestly rather than leaving it open against unresolved unknowns, is the part of G-07's own spec that makes take-over actually INTERACTIVE: the human driving the live session themselves (shell PTY and/or the Steel browser), not just being notified and later marking it complete. Two independent research passes (2026-09-07 and 2026-09-09) converged on the same conclusion: the underlying mechanism for the SHELL half genuinely exists and is well-understood now — execd's own PTY websocket (`/pty/{id}/ws`) defaults to an exclusive, write-capable "holder" mode (stdin/signals/resize), and a new connection can pass `takeover=1` to evict the current holder and become the new one, confirmed by reading execd's actual upstream source rather than guessing. What's still genuinely missing: (1) `LiveAgentPort`'s real production wiring doesn't exist yet even for the READ-ONLY case TASK-171 already built (`liveAgent.routes.ts`'s own header: deliberately left `undefined` in production, a deferred follow-up) — there's no live `role_sandboxes`-backed endpoint resolution to build an interactive path on top of; (2) the BROWSER half (Steel session handoff to the human's own WebSocket, the agent's CDP handle paused) has had zero research done — CDP has no obvious "holder eviction" primitive the way execd's PTY does, and needs its own investigation pass before any design; (3) the authorization/liveness-proof question TASK-188's earlier note raised is unanswered: TASK-171's `onInputDiscarded` mechanically PROVES a viewer connection's input never reaches execd (a real, tested security guarantee) — an interactive mode needs the mirror-image proof, that authorized take-over input DOES reach execd/Steel, and does NOT before authorization or after hand-back, with the same rigor. This is a real, security-relevant design question (ADR-010's enforced set exists precisely because a model must never see a password/2FA/CAPTCHA/payment step), not a routine feature build.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] Real production wiring for `LiveAgentPort` (the read-only case TASK-171 already spec'd) OR confirmation it's covered elsewhere before this task duplicates effort — check first. RESOLVED, and this task's own Description was WRONG about it: `createDatabaseBackedLiveAgent` (`services/control-api/src/ports.ts`) IS genuinely wired into the real production entrypoint — `services/control-api/src/index.ts`'s `start()` (the exact function `dist/index.js` runs) passes `liveAgent: createDatabaseBackedLiveAgent(dbOptions)` into `buildApp`. `liveAgent.routes.ts`'s own header comment claiming this is "left `undefined` in production" was stale — confirmed by direct code trace, not by trusting the comment.
- [x] Shell/PTY interactive mode: a real connection using execd's holder-mode + `takeover=1` contract, with a liveness-proof test mirroring TASK-171's `onInputDiscarded` guarantee in the opposite direction. Built as a deliberately SEPARATE code path from the read-only viewer (`relayTakeover`/`handleTakeoverUpgrade`/`GET /roles/:roleId/live-agent/takeover`, mirroring `relay`/`handleUpgrade`/the viewer's own route exactly in structure) rather than a mode flag threaded through the existing one — a shared function with an "except when this flag is true" branch is exactly the shape of bug that turns "input can never reach execd before authorization" from a hard guarantee into a soft one. `LiveAgentPort.getPtyTakeoverEndpoint` (optional, so an older/view-only port implementation isn't broken) requests `mode=holder&takeover=1`, never `mode=viewer`. `onInputForwarded` is the mirror-image liveness assertion to `onInputDiscarded`, proving real input genuinely reaches execd rather than merely being coded to.
- [~] A real research pass on the Steel/CDP browser-handoff half — split out to **TASK-235** (new), since it is genuinely unresearched and architecturally separate from the shell/PTY mechanism (no CDP "holder eviction" primitive the way execd's PTY has one) — bundling it into this task would have meant either rushing untested design or leaving the shell half's real, working, well-tested build stuck behind it indefinitely.
- [x] `TakeoverCard.onTakeOver` (apps/mobile) opens a genuinely interactive view once built. New `TakeoverScreen` (write-capable terminal: real output display plus a real text input that sends real keystrokes) is exactly what a real `onTakeOver` should navigate to. Found while wiring this, and recorded honestly rather than silently fixed here (out of this task's own scope, TASK-188's own gap, not one this task created): **`TakeoverCard` itself is never actually rendered anywhere in the app** — `grep`-confirmed zero usages outside its own widget file and its own unit test. The card and its `onTakeOver` callback have no live caller for `TakeoverScreen` to be opened FROM yet. Folded into TASK-235 as a prerequisite, since wiring the card into chat is needed for either take-over half (shell or browser) to be reachable by a real user.
- [x] Full suites, lint, typecheck, flutter analyze/test clean.

### TASK-229
**Title:** control-api and worker have zero process supervision — both die on machine restart/logout/crash with no auto-recovery
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** TBD
**Priority:** critical
**Spec_References:** `services/worker/src/main.ts`'s own header comment ("There is, as of this file, still no container/compose entry that runs this — that is a deployment/ops concern this task deliberately leaves open"); live incident 2026-09-09 (this session): a user-reported bot ("jeff") sat unanswered because `control-api` was running a stale build and `worker` had never been started in this environment at all — confirmed directly via `tasklist`/process inspection, not inferred.
**Owned_Paths:** infra/compose/**, docs/runbooks/service-supervision.md (new)
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** Both `services/control-api` and `services/worker` currently exist only as bare foreground processes (`node dist/index.js` / `node dist/main.js`) started by hand in a terminal on a personal Windows dev workstation (Tailscale host `studyworkstation`). Neither has any supervisor: no auto-restart on crash, no start-on-boot, no health check, nothing. If the machine sleeps, restarts, the terminal closes, or nobody remembers to start them, the product is silently down until someone notices — exactly what happened this session. `worker` specifically has never had a real deployment path at all; it was built (TASK-226) with the entrypoint but nothing that keeps it running. Given the existing shared infra box (`clawsrv`, already hosting ~20 unrelated containers) and the R350/month budget ceiling, the likely right shape is real service management — either `pm2`/systemd on `clawsrv` or a docker-compose entry alongside the existing `infra/compose/office/**` pattern — rather than continuing to run production-facing processes as manually-launched terminal jobs on a personal workstation.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] Decide and record the target deployment shape (pm2 vs systemd vs docker-compose, and which host) — a real product-scope/ops decision, not purely mechanical. DECIDED: neither — pm2 was tried first and rejected (see Progress_Notes: accepted both apps as `online` with 0 restarts yet neither ever bound a port or logged a line, reproducibly). Windows Task Scheduler running `infra/compose/service-watchdog.ps1` instead — native, no extra runtime dependency, scoped to this workstation (not a clawsrv/systemd migration, which stays a separate future decision).
- [x] Both `control-api` and `worker` restart automatically on crash and on host reboot, with no manual step. Scheduled Task `OIKONOMOS-ServiceWatchdog`: triggers at logon + every 2 minutes indefinitely, checks control-api (port 3000) and worker (`dist/main.js` on the command line), starts whichever is missing.
- [x] A documented runbook (`docs/runbooks/service-supervision.md`) covering start/stop/status/logs for both services under the chosen supervisor.
- [x] A liveness assertion per CLAUDE.md's control-liveness rule — proven live TWICE: (1) both processes killed by PID, `service-watchdog.ps1` run directly, both restarted, `/health` responded again; (2) both killed again, `schtasks /Run /TN "OIKONOMOS-ServiceWatchdog"` — the REAL scheduled task, not a manual script invocation — both restarted with correct env (`DATABASE_URL` etc.), `/health` responded again. A genuinely healthy pair re-checked produces zero restarts (idempotent, does not thrash).
- [x] The existing manual runbook note updated: `docs/runbooks/service-supervision.md` supersedes the mobile handover's old "must be started manually" instruction; cross-referenced there.
**Branch:** —
**Started_At:** 2026-09-09T17:21:00Z
**Progress_Notes:**
- [2026-09-09T17:21:00Z] [ORCH] Filed after a live incident this session: user reported a bot not replying; root cause traced to `control-api` running a stale build and `worker` never having been started in this environment at all (confirmed via direct process inspection). Both were manually rebuilt and restarted as a same-session fix, but that fix does not survive the next restart/logout — this task is the real one.
- [2026-09-11T20:30:00Z] [ORCH] RESOLVED. Also discovered along the way, worth recording rather than silently working around: the local dev Postgres itself (`infra/compose/docker-compose.local.yml`) was down too when this session started — Docker Desktop wasn't running. Started it, brought the container up, confirmed prior data (jeff's real bot, 2727 roles) survived the recreate. A real, independent finding: even the DATABASE has zero supervision today; Docker Desktop's own "start on login" setting is the documented (manual, one-time) mitigation for that specific piece, recorded as a known limitation in the runbook rather than solved here (out of this task's Owned_Paths — Docker Desktop app settings, not this repo).

  pm2 attempt: installed via `npx pm2`, wrote `infra/compose/ecosystem.config.cjs` with absolute paths (pm2's relative-path `cwd` resolution proved unreliable on Windows — resolved against the wrong base directory on first attempt). Both apps came up `online`, 0 restarts — but neither ever bound a port (`netstat` showed nothing on 3000) nor produced one line of output across `.pm2/logs/*.log`, even after an explicit `pm2 restart`. Reproducible, not a fluke. Rejected; config file deleted rather than left as broken/misleading tooling.

  Real fix: `infra/compose/service-watchdog.ps1` (native PowerShell, no extra dependency) + Windows Scheduled Task `OIKONOMOS-ServiceWatchdog` (`schtasks /Create ... /SC MINUTE /MO 2`; `Register-ScheduledTask` itself returned `Access is denied` even at `-RunLevel Limited` in this environment — the classic `schtasks` CLI form worked without elevation). A real bug was caught during verification: the worker health-check's first version matched `CommandLine -like "*worker*dist*main.js*"`, but a real process's `CommandLine` is literally `"...\node.exe" dist/main.js` — `"worker"` comes from the *working directory*, which `Win32_Process.CommandLine` does not include. That false negative spawned a SECOND, uncoordinated worker process alongside a real live one (confirmed by direct reproduction: two node.exe PIDs both running `dist/main.js`). Fixed to match `*dist*main.js*` alone (unambiguous — only worker has that entrypoint) and re-verified idempotent on a healthy pair afterward.

  Side effect discovered, recorded for TASK-162/231 rather than fixed here: with the real worker now alive persistently for the first time, `services/worker/src/jobs/workerJobQueue.test.ts`'s two pg-boss routine-poll tests failed under a full `pnpm -r test` run — confirmed by direct reproduction that stopping the live worker process makes them pass again immediately. The live worker and the test suite now share one `worker.routine-poll` pg-boss singleton queue name in the same dev database; TASK-221's own root-cause writeup already describes this exact queue as fragile under concurrent access. Not a defect in this task's work — a real, new operational constraint TASK-229 successfully doing its job exposed: running the test suite while the real worker is alive is now a genuine hazard in this shared, uncleaned dev database (same root condition as TASK-231/TASK-162, not yet resolved by either).
**Artifacts:** infra/compose/service-watchdog.ps1, docs/runbooks/service-supervision.md, Windows Scheduled Task `OIKONOMOS-ServiceWatchdog` (host-level, not a repo file)
**Test_Evidence:** Two independent kill-and-revive cycles, the second through the actual deployed Scheduled Task (`schtasks /Run`), both confirmed via `/health` responding again and `tasklist`/`Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` PID inspection. A genuinely healthy pair re-checked is idempotent (0 restarts, correct log lines). A real false-negative bug in the worker health check was caught and fixed during this verification, not before it.

### TASK-230
**Title:** No latency/performance monitoring exists for chat runs — user-reported slowness cannot currently be measured or diagnosed
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** TBD
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** `packages/db/src/runs.ts` (`runs` table already has `started_at`/`ended_at` per row — the raw data exists, nothing reads it for this purpose); user report 2026-09-09 ("when this thing eventually comes up and I ask a question, it usually takes a long time for it to come back with an answer").
**Owned_Paths:** services/control-api/src/metrics.routes.ts (new), packages/db/src/runMetrics.ts (new), apps/dashboard/src/pages/ (metrics view, if in scope)
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** There is currently no visibility into how long a real chat run takes end to end — no logging, no dashboard, no alerting. Investigated 2026-09-09 while diagnosing an unrelated outage: every `runs` row currently in the database is a sub-second test-fixture double from automated test suites, not real LLM traffic, so there is no existing data to even retroactively analyze. Candidate contributors identified by reading the code (not yet measured): the default provider lane is FreeLLMAPI (cost-driven, likely slower/rate-limited than a paid lane), `CapabilityRegistry.build()` reloads connector manifests and re-reads the capability registry from the database on every single run with no caching, and the mobile client polls for new messages rather than receiving a live token stream, which can make a genuinely fast reply feel slow. This task is to instrument first, then optimize against real numbers rather than guesses.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**

**Description:** This session's own `pnpm -r test` run, like apparently many before it, created real rows (roles, threads, tasks, runs) in the shared dev Postgres instance rather than an isolated/transactional test database, and nothing ever cleans them up. Two halves: (1) a one-time cleanup of the current backlog, (2) a structural fix so test runs stop writing permanent rows into a database anyone can query — either a dedicated test-tenant convention with a scheduled purge, or moving DB-backed tests to a genuinely ephemeral database per run.

Real production roles use either a real Firebase UID or the literal constant `"basileia"` — never that shape. Under-deleting is the accepted failure mode, not over-deleting.

- [x] Cross-reference with TASK-162 — see TASK-229's own Progress_Notes for a NEW, related finding this task's cleanup did not resolve: a live worker process and the test suite now contend for the same pg-boss queue in this same shared, uncleaned database. TASK-162 itself not independently re-verified this session (out of scope tonight); this task's conservative selection rule deliberately does not touch the `"basileia"`-tenant rows, so TASK-162's original real-Postgres flake may still reproduce for reasons this cleanup doesn't address.

Deliberately not attempted as a quick fix in that session — deleting rows from a shared database without a verified selection rule is exactly the kind of state change CLAUDE.md's incident-disclosure history in this file's own orchestrator_notes warns against doing unannounced.

Went with the tenant_id rule.

  New `scripts/db-cleanup.mjs`: computes the target tenant set, deletes in FK-dependency order (derived from a live `information_schema` query against every FK referencing `roles`/`tasks`/`runs`/`threads` — 15 tables, children before parents) inside ONE transaction, dry-run by default (`--execute` to commit). `pg` added as a root `devDependency` (wasn't hoisted to root `node_modules` under pnpm's strict linking; a plain `node scripts/db-cleanup.mjs` failed with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` until this was added).

A future task could pursue per-test-file tenant randomization (moving fixtures off the `"basileia"` literal entirely) as the real fix for that remainder — out of scope tonight.

### TASK-236
**Title:** Workspace-1 — dashboard workspace controller: single selection owner, per-thread pending/draft state, message merge, members roster, /workspace/:threadId route
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** specs/OIKONOMOS_WORKSPACE_WAVE_v1.0.md §2.1–§2.7; specs/OIKONOMOS_WORKSPACE_WAVE_v1.0.md §1
**Owned_Paths:** apps/dashboard/src/pages/ChatPage.tsx, apps/dashboard/src/pages/ChatPage.test.tsx, apps/dashboard/src/components/chat/**, apps/dashboard/src/lib/realtime.ts, apps/dashboard/src/lib/realtime.test.ts, apps/dashboard/src/lib/workspaceState.ts, apps/dashboard/src/lib/workspaceState.test.ts, apps/dashboard/src/App.tsx, apps/dashboard/src/App.test.tsx
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** Fix the four confirmed dashboard defects and the page-boundary gap with one controlled state module. Today `ChatPage.tsx:116` and `ChatShell.tsx:54-64` each own `activeBotId`; the parent's `handleSelectBot` (`ChatPage.tsx:177-191`) never calls its own setter, so the SSE effect (`ChatPage.tsx:219-253`) and the routines lookup stay on the first thread while the child renders another. `isBotResponding`/`pendingSinceRef` are one value for all threads (`ChatPage.tsx:119,125,179-181`). `ComposeBox` holds one draft, never remounts on switch, and clears before the void `handleSend` resolves (`ComposeBox.tsx:18-25`, `ChatPage.tsx:297`), so a failed POST loses the text. `ChatPage.tsx:292` passes `members={[]}` and the Members tab is the right panel's default, so it is permanently empty; the sidebar's create-bot dialog works but the thread list is never refreshed after creation.

  Approach: introduce `apps/dashboard/src/lib/workspaceState.ts` (a reducer/hook keyed by threadId holding `messages`, `pending`, `draft`, `lastSeenMessageId`) owned by `ChatPage`; make `ChatShell`/`ComposeBox` fully controlled (`activeThreadId`, `draft`, `onDraftChange` props; no internal `useState` copies). Merge messages by id and never let a slower history fetch overwrite streamed messages. Add `/workspace/:threadId` in `App.tsx`; `/` redirects to the most recent thread. Fetch the roster (`listRoles()` already returns it — `ChatPage.tsx:153` discards it) and refresh threads after create. Keep tab close, run cancel, routine pause and mark-read as distinct actions (§1). Do NOT touch `lib/api.ts`, `AuthContext.tsx` or `LoginPage.tsx` — those belong to TASK-239/241, which follow this task with the same owner.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] Exactly one component owns the active thread id; `ChatShell` and `ComposeBox` have no internal copy of it (grep: no `useState` for activeBotId/activeThreadId below `ChatPage`). (§2.1)
- [x] Switching A→B→C→A in a three-thread fixture: the rendered transcript, the open SSE stream URL, the composer's send target and the routines panel's role all change together on every switch — asserted in `ChatPage.test.tsx` with a multi-thread fixture and a fake stream. (§2.1, §2.7)
- [x] Pending/'responding' state is per thread: a bot frame arriving on thread B while A is active neither clears nor sets A's pending state; reopening B shows B's state. (§2.2)
- [x] Drafts are per thread, kept in memory only: text typed in A is absent from B and present again on returning to A; a failed `POST /threads/:id/messages` (fake 500) leaves the draft and shows an error; a 2xx clears only that thread's draft. (§2.3)
- [x] A history response that resolves after a streamed message arrived does not remove the streamed message; messages are deduplicated by id. Switching threads closes the previous stream (asserted on the fake reader's cancel). (§2.4)
- [x] The Members panel shows the server roster for the active thread; creating a bot or group from the sidebar refreshes the thread list without reload. (§2.5)
- [x] `/workspace/:threadId` renders that thread; a 404 renders a not-found state; `/` redirects to the most recent thread or empty state. (§2.6)
- [x] `pnpm --filter @oikonomos/dashboard test`, typecheck and build green; full `pnpm -r test` run recorded in Test_Evidence.

**Description:** Three small routes and one bounded projection. (a) `GET /auth/me` → 200 `{tenantId, kind: 'service'|'user', expiresAt}` for a valid `control_api_session` cookie or bearer, 401 otherwise — the cookie is `HttpOnly` (`auth.ts:75-77`) so the dashboard cannot self-check and today always starts logged out. (c) `GET /workspace/summary` → one row per thread the principal owns (reuse `findTenantOwnedThread`'s ownership rule; a group thread is owned only if every member role is): `{threadId, latestRun: {runId, status}|null, pendingApprovals, lastActivityAt}`. Derive `latestRun` from the thread's newest `messages.run_id` joined to `runs`, and `pendingApprovals` from `approvals` with `status='pending'` on that run — no new association table. Put the SQL in `packages/db/src/workspaceSummary.ts` behind a port on `ChatDependencies` in `ports.ts` (interface + database-backed implementation only; do not touch the `runChatTask` composition at `ports.ts:393`, TASK-238 owns that next). Add an index migration only if `EXPLAIN` shows a seq scan on `messages(run_id)` or `approvals(run_id,status)`; record the plan in Progress_Notes either way. (d) `GET /health` gains `buildSha` (read from `OIKONOMOS_BUILD_SHA` env or `git rev-parse` at start, never at request time). (e) Replace the stale paragraph at `liveAgent.routes.ts:35-44` that says production wiring is deferred — `index.ts:42` wires it; this is a comment-only edit in that file. Tests go in new files (`session.routes.test.ts`, `workspace.routes.test.ts`) — `chat.routes.test.ts` belongs to blocked TASK-162, do not edit it. 404-never-403 discipline throughout.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] `GET /auth/me` returns 200 with tenant id and expiry for a session minted by `/auth/login` and by `/auth/google` (fake verifier), 401 with no body detail for a missing, expired or tampered cookie. (§3.1)

- [x] `GET /workspace/summary` returns exactly one row per owned thread with `latestRun`, `pendingApprovals`, `lastActivityAt`; a thread with no runs has `latestRun: null`; another principal's threads never appear (real-Postgres two-principal test, FK-ordered cleanup in `finally`). (§4.1)

### TASK-238
**Title:** Workspace-1 — run concurrency gate: global cap of two executing runs, per-role serialisation, visible queued reason, liveness assertion
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** CX9
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** specs/OIKONOMOS_WORKSPACE_WAVE_v1.0.md §5.1–§5.4; CLAUDE.md control-liveness rule; ADR-005
**Owned_Paths:** services/worker/src/runConcurrency.ts, services/worker/src/runConcurrency.test.ts, services/worker/src/index.ts, services/control-api/src/ports.ts, services/control-api/src/ports.test.ts, services/control-api/src/index.ts
**Depends_On:** TASK-237
**Description:** No cap or serialisation exists today: control-api fires runs as `void deps.runChatTask(...)` (`app.ts:1738,1756,2131`) through `ports.ts:393` `runChatTask: (request) => chatRunDriver.run(request)`; pg-boss carries only heartbeat and routine-poll; the budget gate is documented TOCTOU (`subprocessProviders.ts:109-122`). Owner decision D4: two concurrent runs, per-role serialisation. Build `services/worker/src/runConcurrency.ts`: an in-process gate `createRunGate({maxConcurrent: 2})` exposing `run(roleId, fn)` that serialises per role and caps globally, FIFO, never drops, and emits a `run.queued` audit event (run id, role id, position, reason `concurrency.cap`) when it queues — that event is the liveness evidence. Wrap the `runChatTask` composition in `ports.ts` with the gate (this task owns `ports.ts` after TASK-237 merges). The queued reason must be visible in the run's audit trail. Group fan-out (`groupFanout.ts`) goes through the same `runChatTask` port and is therefore covered; assert it. Do not change `runChatTask`'s signature. Sequenced after TASK-237 because both touch `ports.ts`.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] With the gate at 2, three runs submitted for three roles: two start immediately, the third starts only after one finishes; asserted with controllable fake `runChatTask` promises. (§5.1, §5.3)
- [x] Two runs for the same role never execute concurrently even when the global cap has room. (§5.2)
- [x] A queued run is never dropped: submitting ten runs completes all ten in FIFO order per role. (§5.3)
- [x] Liveness: the third submission produces a `run.queued` audit event with reason `concurrency.cap`; a separate test builds the production `ports.ts` composition and proves the gate is in the path by observing that event, not by inspecting config. (§5.4)
- [x] Group-thread fan-out runs are subject to the same gate (test through `deliverBotToBotMessage` or the fan-out port). (§5.2)
- [x] worker and control-api suites green; `pnpm -r test` recorded.

**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** CX9
**Priority:** medium
**Spec_References:** specs/OIKONOMOS_WORKSPACE_WAVE_v1.0.md §9.2; ADR-007 replay window; ADR-001
**Owned_Paths:** services/worker/src/jobs/**, services/worker/src/runLifecycle.ts, services/worker/src/runLifecycle.test.ts, services/worker/test/runLifecycle.test.ts, services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts, services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.test.ts, services/worker/src/main.ts, services/worker/src/main.test.ts, services/worker/src/groupFanout.ts, services/worker/src/groupFanout.test.ts, services/worker/src/index.ts, packages/db/src/tasks.ts, packages/db/src/tasks.test.ts, packages/db/src/index.ts, infra/postgres/migrations/025_task_execution.up.sql, infra/postgres/migrations/025_task_execution.down.sql, services/control-api/src/ports.ts, services/control-api/src/index.ts, services/control-api/src/app.ts, services/control-api/src/app.test.ts, services/control-api/src/chat.routes.test.ts
**Depends_On:** TASK-238, TASK-242, TASK-244
**Description:** Today `reconcileInterruptedRuns` (`runLifecycle.ts:224-250`) → `resumeInterruptedRun` (`:47-55`) → `resumeRun` is a status flip; pg-boss registers only heartbeat and routine-poll (`workerJobQueue.ts:6-7`); chat runs are in-process promises fired from control-api. A restart loses the in-flight turn. Design first: an ADR (protected path, different-model review) deciding queue-driven run execution — job per run, singleton per run id, the TASK-238 gate becomes the consumer's concurrency, reconciliation re-enqueues rather than re-labels, governed side effects stay exactly-once via the approval nonce, anything else re-executed must be idempotent or parked. Build after the ADR is accepted. Unblocks the full A15 case.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] ADR-016 accepted after different-model review, stating the queue, the re-enqueue rule, and the exactly-once boundary. (§9.2)
- [x] Killing the worker during a safe test run and restarting it results in the run reaching a real executor turn and a result, with no duplicate governed side effect (approval consumed once). (§9.2, A15)
- [x] A run parked on approval stays parked across restart and resumes only through the normal decide path. (ADR-007)
- [x] Liveness: reconciliation emits a `run.requeued` audit event; a test keys on it.

### TASK-253
**Title:** Connector minters cannot consume a dynamically-vaulted secret — per-role/run-scoped minter resolution design + implementation (ADR-014 Amendment 2026-09-14, phase 2)
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** CX9
**Priority:** medium
**Spec_References:** docs/decisions/ADR-014-dynamic-secret-vault.md §1, Amendment 2026-09-14; TASK-250 Progress_Notes and dossier (full live evidence already gathered — read before re-deriving it)
**Owned_Paths:** — design-first: this changes chatRunDriver.ts's minter composition from shared-pool to scoped-per-request; needs a design decision before any file is touched; see Description
**Depends_On:** TASK-250
**Description:** TASK-250 (phase 1) makes a human-fulfilled secret genuinely encrypted, stored, and audited via `secretVault`, but confirmed there is no way for a connector session minter to actually use one: `services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts:211-247` builds one shared, role-agnostic minter pool per connector at worker composition time, and each minter is wired to `packages/connectors/src/mcp/envSecretResolver.ts`, which only resolves fixed manifest-declared `secret://mcp/.../…` refs backed by static `OIK_SECRET_*` env vars. A vault-minted `secret://<uuid>` ref is bound to one role (and implicitly one request), so it cannot be cached into a pool shared across every run of every role without either (a) a real risk of cross-role/cross-run secret leakage if the pool is looked up by connector name alone, or (b) scoping the pool per (role, run) instead of per connector — a genuine architectural change to how `chatRunDriver.ts` composes minters, not a resolver addition. Design first: does a role-scoped resolver need to be constructed fresh per run (cost/latency of a new minter per turn) or can it be cached per (tenant, role) safely (what does "safely" require — a proof that a stale cached minter cannot outlive a revoked/rotated dynamic secret)? Which connector(s) are the first real consumer — likely none yet, since no manifest currently declares a role-grant expecting a dynamic secret; confirm whether this is genuinely needed before a connector's manifest asks for it, or whether it's premature to build.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] A design note (Progress_Notes or a short doc) answering: per-run vs per-(tenant,role) caching, staleness/revocation handling, and which connector (if any) currently has a real, named use case — do not build speculative infrastructure with no consumer.

**Status:** done

**Priority:** medium
**Spec_References:** `packages/db/src/database.test.ts:79-95` (the "Database role grants — list/upsert/revoke (TASK-119)" integration suite and its `cleanup()` helper); `packages/broker/src/capabilityRegistry.ts:136`'s `StaleCapabilityRowError` (the downstream symptom, working as designed, not itself a bug)

**Description:** Confirmed independently TWICE this session by two separately-dispatched, identity-confirmed review agents (TASK-227 and TASK-253 reviews), both against a freshly-serialized `scripts/test-isolated.ps1` run with no concurrent contention — this is a real, reproducible, pre-existing bug, not flakiness or a review artifact. Verbatim error: `update or delete on table "capabilities" violates foreign key constraint "role_grants_capability_id_fkey" on table "role_grants"`, thrown from `cleanup()`'s own `DELETE FROM capabilities WHERE capability_id = ANY($1)` step (`database.test.ts:92`). `cleanup()` scopes its `role_grants`/`roles` deletes to one fixed `roleId` (`task-119-grants-suite-role`) before deleting the two fixture capabilities — read directly, no other role in this same file references `capabilityA`/`capabilityB` by name, so the blocking `role_grants` row is left behind by something outside what's visible in a single read of this file: either a genuinely concurrent second invocation of this suite (Vitest file-level parallelism against the same shared DB), a prior run's row that a preceding cleanup pass didn't reach, or another mechanism not yet identified. Once the two fixture `capabilities` rows survive a run, `CapabilityRegistry.build`'s fail-closed check (correct broker behavior, not a defect) throws `StaleCapabilityRowError` against them for every subsequent script in the same `scripts/test-isolated.ps1` invocation, cascading into large, misleading-looking failure counts in `evals/harness` and `services/worker` that have cost real review time twice already (both reviews had to trace the cascade back to this one root cause before trusting an unrelated branch was clean).
**Acceptance_Criteria:**

- [x] `cleanup()` (and any equivalent pattern elsewhere in this file, e.g. the TASK-140 suite immediately below it) made resilient to a pre-existing FK-referencing row — either scope the capability delete correctly so it never contends, or make the whole cleanup idempotent/order-safe regardless of what state a prior run left behind.

### TASK-258
**Title:** Scheduled routine firings never actually execute — `routineJob.ts`'s poll path creates an orphaned task row and never enqueues a real run (a genuine "lost accepted work" hold condition)
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** critical
**Spec_References:** `services/worker/src/jobs/routineJob.ts:111-118` (the `createTask` port passed to `scheduler.fireRoutine`, calling only `@oikonomos/db`'s bare `createTask` -- no run, no queue enqueue); `services/control-api/src/ports.ts:531-541`'s `testRunRoutine` (the CORRECT reference implementation: creates the task, then calls `notify({task, threadId})`, which is what actually creates a real run and enqueues `worker.run-execution`); TASK-246/ADR-016 (`submitTaskExecution`, the atomic task+run+queue path this should have been wired through); GROKBOT-RESEARCH-DOCS/OIKONOMOS_RELEASE_ACCEPTANCE_2026-09-16.md's A19/A12 pass conditions ("Scheduled task produces actual work") and its own hold-condition list ("lost accepted work").
**Owned_Paths:** services/worker/src/jobs/routineJob.ts, services/worker/src/jobs/routineJob.test.ts
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** Found live during TASK-245's A19 acceptance case (2026-09-15), while investigating why a real, correctly-scheduled test routine's task never produced a run. Root-caused precisely by comparing two code paths side by side: `services/control-api/src/ports.ts`'s `testRunRoutine` (the manual "test run" button, POST /routines/:id/test-run) creates a task via `dbCreateTask` and then explicitly calls `notify({task, threadId})` -- the real mechanism (`notifyAfterChatRun`) that creates a run and enqueues it for execution. `services/worker/src/jobs/routineJob.ts`'s own scheduled-fire path (the REAL automatic cron-driven mechanism this whole product feature depends on) calls ONLY `createTask(options, {...})` from `@oikonomos/db` directly -- a bare database insert with no run creation and no `worker.run-execution` enqueue whatsoever. The resulting task row has no run, ever, and nothing else in the system reconciles a run-less task (`reconcileInterruptedRuns` only reconciles existing runs in an open status, not tasks that never got a run at all) -- the orphaning is permanent, not self-healing. Confirmed directly against live data during this session's own A19 test: a real routine fired at 2026-09-15T05:00:24Z, `last_fire_status` recorded `queued`, a real task row was created, and it never produced a run or any pg-boss job at all, even after the routine's own next poll cycle and after an unrelated large stale-queue backlog was cleared -- ruling out queue congestion as the cause and confirming this as the actual root cause. **This means every automatically-scheduled routine execution in this deployed environment has likely never actually run since routines were introduced** -- a core, advertised feature (§9.3, unattended scheduled work) is completely non-functional via its real, unattended trigger path; only the manual "test run" button works.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] `routineJob.ts`'s `createTask` port calls the real, atomic execution path (either `submitTaskExecution` directly, or mirrors `testRunRoutine`'s `dbCreateTask` + `notify({task, threadId})` pattern) so a scheduled fire genuinely creates a run and enqueues `worker.run-execution`, not just a task row.
- [x] A real, non-mocked liveness test: a routine with a due `next_fire_at` is polled, and the test asserts a REAL run row exists afterward with a REAL `worker.run-execution` pg-boss job enqueued for it -- not just that `createTask` was called.
- [x] Confirm whether any currently-orphaned real (non-test-fixture) routine-fired tasks exist in the live database from before this fix, and if so, whether they need manual remediation (out of this task's own scope to silently backfill without a decision, but must be named here for whoever picks this up).
- [x] Full `pnpm -r test` via `scripts/test-isolated.ps1` recorded.

### TASK-259
**Title:** `GET /threads/:id/stream`'s SSE connection never re-validates its session after the initial handshake, so an expired session cannot be forced to stop an already-open stream
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** medium
**Spec_References:** `services/control-api/src/app.ts:1655-1729` (the `/threads/:id/stream` route: `request.tenantId` is resolved once at connection time by the auth `preHandler`, then the poll (`pollIntervalMs`, default 300ms) and heartbeat (15s) timers run indefinitely using that already-resolved value with no re-check); `services/control-api/src/auth.ts`'s `SESSION_TTL_MS` (24 hours); specs/OIKONOMOS_WORKSPACE_WAVE_v1.0.md's A06 acceptance case ("expired session cannot continue sockets" is an explicit, named pass condition).
**Owned_Paths:** services/control-api/src/app.ts, services/control-api/test/app.test.ts
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** Found live during TASK-245's A06 acceptance case (2026-09-15). The SSE stream route's authentication is checked exactly once, at the initial HTTP handshake (via the shared auth `preHandler` that sets `request.tenantId`) -- the same closure keeps using that resolved value for the lifetime of the connection. Neither the 300ms poll timer nor the 15s heartbeat timer re-verifies the originating session cookie's signature or expiry. This means a session that legitimately opened a stream and then expires (24h TTL) while the connection stays open will keep receiving real-time thread messages indefinitely past its nominal expiry, until the client itself disconnects or the socket errors. This is NOT a cross-principal breach at connection time (the connection was genuinely authorized when opened) -- it is a session-lifetime enforcement gap on an already-legitimately-opened long-lived connection, lower urgency than a fresh unauthorized-access bug, but still a real, disclosed gap against this exact acceptance case's own named pass condition.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] The SSE route re-validates the originating session (signature + expiry) on some real, bounded interval (e.g. once per heartbeat tick, or via a dedicated timer keyed to the session's own `expiresAt`) and force-closes the connection (`cleanup()`) the moment it is no longer valid.
- [x] A real, non-mocked test: open a stream with a session set to expire in `N` ms, advance time (or use a short real TTL) past that point, and assert the connection is actually closed by the server -- not merely that a NEW connection attempt would be rejected (already covered elsewhere).
- [x] Confirmed `liveAgent`/`browserTakeover` (WebSocket upgrades, no `setInterval` poll/heartbeat loop, structurally different from SSE) have the same class of gap but need their own fix shape -- scoped this task to SSE only, filed TASK-286 for the WebSocket routes rather than silently widen or ignore.
- [x] Full `pnpm -r test` via `scripts/test-isolated.ps1` recorded (isolated control-api: 24/24 files, 306/306 tests; full recursive run shows only pre-existing, unrelated services/worker failures, confirmed by clean git status on that package).

### TASK-260
**Title:** Logout is completely broken in production — every real logout request fails with 400 before the route handler runs, so the session cookie is never actually revoked
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** CX9
**Priority:** critical
**Spec_References:** `apps/dashboard/src/lib/api.ts:37-43`'s shared `request()` helper (unconditionally sets `content-type: application/json` on every call, including a bodyless request); `apps/dashboard/src/lib/api.ts:118-120`'s `logout()` (`POST /auth/logout` with no body at all); `services/control-api/src/app.ts:1078-1082`'s `/auth/logout` route (no schema, would work correctly if it were ever reached); Fastify's own default JSON body parser, which rejects a request declaring `content-type: application/json` with zero bytes of body as `400 FST_ERR_CTP_EMPTY_JSON_BODY` -- this happens in Fastify's own body-parsing hook, BEFORE the route handler (and therefore before `revokedSessionTokens.revoke(token)` and the expired-cookie response) ever runs; specs/OIKONOMOS_WORKSPACE_WAVE_v1.0.md's A05 acceptance case ("logout clears private UI state").
**Owned_Paths:** apps/dashboard/src/lib/api.ts
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** Found live during TASK-245's A05 acceptance case (2026-09-15). Confirmed with certainty, not inferred: `curl -X POST https://.../auth/logout -H "Content-Type: application/json"` (matching exactly what the dashboard's own shared `request()` helper sends for every call, logout included) returns `400 {"statusCode":400,"code":"FST_ERR_CTP_EMPTY_JSON_BODY","message":"Body cannot be empty when content-type is set to 'application/json'"}`. This means `services/control-api/src/app.ts`'s `/auth/logout` route handler -- which correctly calls `revokedSessionTokens.revoke(token)` and sets an expired `Set-Cookie` header -- **has never actually executed for any real logout click**, because Fastify's own body parser rejects the request before routing reaches it. Live evidence from a real browser session: after clicking "Log out," the dashboard's `AuthContext.logout()` still flips its own local `isAuthenticated` state to `false` inside a `finally` block regardless of the server's response, so the UI visually redirects to the login screen and LOOKS like logout succeeded -- but the real session cookie is never cleared and was never server-side revoked. A direct `GET /auth/me` using the same browser context, performed entirely outside the React app immediately after the visible "logout," still returned `200 {"tenantId":"basileia","kind":"user",...}` -- the session remains fully valid for its full 24-hour lifetime. **This is a genuine, previously-undiscovered security defect**: any user who believes they have logged out (for example on a shared or public device) has not actually ended their session, and anyone with continued access to that browser or a copied session cookie can keep using it until natural expiry, indistinguishable from a still-logged-in session. Also confirmed the identical failure on `POST /routines/:id/pause` and `/resume` (the same request shape the client's `pauseRoutine`/`resumeRoutine` helpers send) -- this is not an isolated logout-only defect, it breaks every bodyless call made through the shared `request()` helper, corroborating and explaining TASK-256's original (since-addended) finding that a routine cannot actually be paused through the real product.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] `logout()` (and any other bodyless call using the shared `request()` helper) either omits the `content-type: application/json` header when there is no body, or sends a real empty JSON body (`{}`) so Fastify's parser accepts it -- fix at the shared helper level if other bodyless calls exist, not just this one call site.
- [x] A real, non-mocked test: a genuine `POST /auth/logout` call (through the actual client helper, not a hand-rolled fetch) returns `204`, and an immediately following `GET /auth/me` with the same cookie returns `401` -- proving the round trip end to end, not just that the request no longer 400s.
- [x] Audit confirmed complete: exactly four bodyless calls in `apps/dashboard/src/lib/api.ts` share this defect -- `logout()`, `pauseRoutine()`, `resumeRoutine()`, `testRunRoutine()` (every other POST call in this file already sends a real JSON body and is unaffected). Fix all four in this task.
- [x] `flutter`/dashboard equivalent checked too if the mobile client's own logout call has the same shape -- name it here even if this task's Owned_Paths only covers the dashboard fix.
- [x] Full `pnpm -r test` via `scripts/test-isolated.ps1` recorded.

**Started_At:** 2026-09-15T10:15:00Z
**Progress_Notes:**

See `docs/acceptance/workspace-1/A05-session-logout.md` for the full account, including the raw HTTP evidence (cookie presence before/after, direct GET /auth/me bypassing all client-side logic).

### TASK-269
**Title:** CRITICAL -- an ordinary follow-up chat message never continues the previous Claude session; every turn in a conversation starts completely fresh with zero memory of anything said before it
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** critical
**Spec_References:** `services/control-api/src/app.ts`'s `POST /threads/:id/messages` (1:1 and group-with-one-recipient branches, ~lines 1926-1943 and ~1899-1917); `services/control-api/src/ports.ts`'s `submitTaskExecution`/`runChatTask` (neither ever looks up a prior run's `session_ref`); `services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts` lines ~340-360, ~446, ~787 (the ONLY place `--resume` is ever attached to the Claude CLI invocation is `request.resume`, which is set exclusively by the interrupted-run-reconciliation/approval-resume path, never by an ordinary new message in an existing thread).
**Owned_Paths:** packages/db/src/runs.ts, packages/db/src/runs.test.ts, packages/db/src/index.ts, services/control-api/src/app.ts, services/control-api/src/ports.ts, services/control-api/src/chat.routes.test.ts, services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts, services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.test.ts
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** Found live (2026-09-16) via direct owner-reported symptom: a real bot (`maximus`, Claude provider) completely lost track of its own conversation across ordinary turns -- asked for information already given two messages earlier, denied seeing a question it had just asked itself, and treated a bare follow-up word ("cape town") as meaningless out-of-context input. Root-caused precisely, not inferred: `POST /threads/:id/messages`'s real 1:1 chat path (`app.ts`) always builds a brand-new `taskInput` and calls `submitTaskExecution`/`createTask`+`runChatTask` with NO `resume` field -- there is no code anywhere in this path that looks up the thread's own most recent prior run to continue it. `chatRunDriver.ts`'s doc comment for the Gemini lane explicitly says Claude relies on the Agent SDK's own `--resume` instead of manual history reconstruction (unlike Gemini, which correctly rebuilds full history from persisted messages every turn via `buildGeminiTurnPrompt` -- confirmed still correct, not in scope here) -- but nothing ever computes or passes that `--resume` token for an ordinary continued conversation. `request.resume` is set ONLY by the narrow interrupted-run-reconciliation/post-approval-resume path (a completely different scenario: continuing ONE specific run after a pause, not turn-to-turn conversation continuity). The result: `chatRunDriver.ts`'s `claudePrintCommand` never receives a `--resume` argument for a normal follow-up message, so the Claude CLI starts a genuinely fresh, memoryless session on every single turn. This is almost certainly true for EVERY Claude-provider bot in this product, not just the one it was caught on -- it is a foundational chat-continuity gap, not a one-off. The underlying infrastructure needed to fix this already exists and works (the role's own sandbox persists correctly across turns via pause/resume -- confirmed independently and freshly this same session during TASK-262's diagnostic) -- this is a missing wiring step, not a deeper architectural gap.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] Add a real DB helper (e.g. `getLatestRunForThread` in `packages/db/src/runs.ts`) that finds the most recent run for a given thread (join through `tasks`, order by `started_at DESC`, `LIMIT 1`) -- do not assume `listRuns`'s existing filters cover this, they don't (checked: `listRuns` filters by `tenantId`/`status`/`taskId`/`cursor` only, no `threadId`/`roleId` filter exists today).
- [x] Wire this into `app.ts`'s `POST /threads/:id/messages` (both the 1:1 branch and the group-with-one-real-recipient branch -- read both before deciding whether the fan-out/multi-recipient branch needs the same treatment or has genuinely different continuity semantics per-recipient; do not guess, check what each recipient's own prior run in this thread looks like): when a prior run exists for this thread, pass its `sessionRef ?? runId` as the new run's `resume.sessionRef` so `chatRunDriver.ts`'s existing `--resume` plumbing picks it up -- this may mean widening `runChatTask`'s/`submitTaskExecution`'s own input shape if the current `resume` field's semantics (built for the interrupted-run case) don't cleanly cover "continue the thread's last completed run with a NEW task/run row," not just "resume this exact same run" -- investigate `startTaskRun`/`createTaskExecutionRun`'s actual session_ref handling before assuming either shape fits, and design the smallest correct change rather than forcing the existing `resume` field to mean two different things.
- [x] Correctly do NOT resume when: there is no prior run for this thread (first message ever -- must start fresh, not error); the prior run's resolved provider differs from the current one (a mid-conversation provider switch must never hand a resume token to a provider that doesn't understand it -- this exact danger is already named in this file's own existing comments, cite and respect it).
- [x] A real, non-mocked, end-to-end test: send two REAL sequential chat messages through the actual `/threads/:id/messages` route to a real running worker (real Claude provider, real spend -- keep it minimal, e.g. "my favorite color is teal" then "what did I just tell you my favorite color was"), and assert the SECOND turn's real model reply correctly references information ONLY present in the first turn. This is the one acceptance bar that actually matters -- a test that only checks "a resume argument was passed" without proving the model actually remembered something is not sufficient evidence this bug is fixed.
- [x] Full `pnpm -r test` via `scripts/test-isolated.ps1` recorded.
- [x] Dossier states plainly whether this same gap affects the group/fan-out chat path too (multiple recipients in one thread) -- if it does, name it explicitly rather than silently fixing only the 1:1 case and leaving the multi-recipient case's own continuity gap undiscovered a second time.
